strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP problem: exploiting slot annotations to improve task-oriented utterance embeddings. The combination of template augmentation, template contrastive learning, and utterance–template alignment is coherent and computationally accessible with BERT-base.

The results provide promising evidence of improvement beyond augmentation alone. Table 2 reports average accuracy of 83.87 for TaDSE with MLP versus 81.42 for SimCSE trained on the augmented data. Table 4 usefully separates the contributions of template and pairwise losses.

Evaluation covers five intent-classification datasets, including automatically extracted, noisy entities on CLINC150. The augmentation experiments and explicit reporting of unsuccessful compression results provide useful information about the method’s limitations.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is insufficiently specified. The manuscript omits the three contrastive temperatures, optimizer details, and precise pooling/MLP configuration. The validation splits and construction of the 'full utterance/template' nearest-neighbor reference set also need clarification, including whether every baseline uses the same reference candidates and whether compression requires gold test-time slots. With code deferred until acceptance, these omissions materially limit independent verification.

Experimental reliability remains uncertain. Appendix D uses test-set learning curves to motivate training-duration choices, while validation-based selection is explicitly described only for the compression coefficient. The paper should establish that all configuration selection was independent of test results. No repeated-run variability or confidence intervals are reported, making small improvements difficult to assess. Training single-source MLP variants for eight epochs versus two for other models also confounds attribution of their gains to the MLP.

The supervision and annotation-efficiency claims need qualification. Four datasets supply human slot annotations, and CLINC150 uses a pretrained NER model; this is not annotation-free learning, although it avoids sentence-pair labels. Moreover, evaluation retrieves from the full labeled training set, so the motivation concerning limited annotations is not directly tested. Annotation-budget experiments would substantiate that motivation.

The interpretation of semantic compression exceeds the evidence. Interpolation toward a shared template mechanically reduces distances between utterances sharing that template before renormalization; normalization of the mixed vectors is not specified. Consequently, improved alignment alone does not establish improved semantic structure or validate the optimal coefficient as a measure of semantic well-formedness. The t-SNE plots remain qualitative, and Table 5 shows small gains on SNIPS/ATIS alongside degradation on MASSIVE/CLINC150.

The broad state-of-the-art and realistic-augmentation claims need stronger support or narrower wording. The principal comparisons use older embedding methods, while contemporary API comparisons cover only two datasets. Naturalness and preservation of intent under slot substitution are not directly measured. These limitations constrain the broader contribution; the unresolved evaluation and reproducibility issues are the decisive reasons the recommendation remains borderline Findings.
